questions.stem: A refinery has a surplus of decane (C₁₀H₂₂) but high demand for petrol and ethene. Decane is cracked to produce octane and ethene. What is the balanced equation?

options.text: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₂
C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄
C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₆ + C₂H₆
C₁₀H₂₂ → C₅H₁₂ + C₅H₁₂

questions.explanation: Cracking breaks a long-chain alkane into a shorter alkane and an alkene. Balancing: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. Check: 10C = 8C + 2C, and 22H = 18H + 4H. Octane (C₈H₁₈) is used in petrol, and ethene (C₂H₄) is used to make poly(ethene) and other chemicals. This is how cracking solves the supply-demand mismatch.

questions.stem: There are two main methods of cracking: catalytic cracking and steam cracking. Catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at about 500°C, while steam cracking uses higher temperatures (over 800°C) with steam. Which method typically produces more alkenes?

options.text: Catalytic cracking produces more alkenes
Both produce identical products
Steam cracking at higher temperatures tends to produce a higher proportion of alkenes like ethene
Neither method produces alkenes

questions.explanation: Steam cracking at high temperatures (800-900°C) tends to produce a higher proportion of short-chain alkenes (ethene, propene), which are valuable for making polymers and other chemicals. Catalytic cracking at lower temperatures with a zeolite catalyst tends to produce more branched alkanes suitable for petrol. The choice of method depends on which products are in greater demand.

questions.stem: After cracking, a mixture of products is obtained. How could you test whether one of the products is an alkene rather than an alkane?

options.text: Add universal indicator — alkenes are acidic
Add bromine water — it will decolourise if the product is an alkene
Measure the density — alkenes are always denser
Burn it — only alkanes will burn

questions.explanation: Bromine water (orange) decolourises when added to an alkene because bromine adds across the C=C double bond in an addition reaction. Alkanes do not react with bromine water at room temperature, so the solution stays orange. This is the standard chemical test to distinguish unsaturated compounds (alkenes) from saturated ones (alkanes).

questions.stem: Ethene produced from cracking is used to make poly(ethene), ethanol, and many other chemicals. It is often called the most important organic chemical in industry. Why is ethene so versatile?

options.text: It is the only gas produced from crude oil
Its C=C double bond is reactive and can undergo addition reactions with many different reagents
It is the most abundant fraction from distillation
It has the highest energy content of any hydrocarbon

questions.explanation: Ethene's C=C double bond makes it highly reactive. It can undergo addition reactions with hydrogen (to make ethane), water/steam (to make ethanol), halogens (to make halogenoalkanes), hydrogen halides, and itself (polymerisation to make poly(ethene)). This versatility as a chemical building block (feedstock) makes it the most important industrial organic chemical.

questions.stem: A student heats liquid paraffin (a long-chain alkane mixture) over aluminium oxide catalyst in the laboratory. Gas collects over water and decolourises bromine water. What has happened?

options.text: The paraffin has evaporated without any chemical change
The paraffin has undergone cracking, producing gaseous alkenes that decolourise bromine water
The aluminium oxide has reacted with the paraffin
Water has reacted with the paraffin to produce an acid

questions.explanation: The aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) acts as a catalyst for catalytic cracking. The long-chain alkanes in liquid paraffin break down into shorter molecules, including gaseous alkenes. The fact that the collected gas decolourises bromine water confirms the presence of alkenes (with C=C double bonds). This is a standard school laboratory demonstration of cracking.
